package_info.why_malicious: The described attack technique involves uploading a benign source distribution and wheels, then later uploading a malicious, highly specific wheel (e.g., for a particular platform/architecture). This wheel could contain malicious code or dependencies, but would only be installed on matching systems, making detection much harder. The overall package appears benign, but a subset of users receive a malicious artifact.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: setup.py or embedded malicious dependency in the wheel (not shown in the report, but implied: e.g., a dependency or code block that exfiltrates data or executes arbitrary code during install)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the code executes arbitrary Python instructions (e.g., exfiltrates environment variables or runs a reverse shell) only when the specific wheel is installed, targeting a narrow set of users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The wheel is platform-specific and uploaded after the initial benign release, increasing the likelihood it is intended to target a specific victim or environment. The code or dependency is only present in this wheel, not in the source or other wheels.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is for all wheels and the source distribution to be functionally equivalent and uploaded together. Uploading a new, more specific wheel later with different (potentially malicious) content violates this expectation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use: uploading platform-specific wheels for performance optimizations or binary compatibility, but the code/content should remain consistent with the source.
key_indicators: Highly specific wheel uploaded after initial release
Wheel content differs from source distribution
Malicious dependency or code only present in one wheel

attack_chain.action: Upload a benign source distribution and wheels to PyPI, passing all static analysis and review.
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishes trust and widespread adoption of the package.

attack_chain.action: Upload a new, highly specific wheel (e.g., black-24.4.0-cp312-cp312-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl) containing malicious code or dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: Targets only users/installations matching the specific platform/architecture.

attack_chain.action: When a user on the targeted platform installs the package, the malicious code executes at install-time.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious payload is executed, achieving the attacker's goal (e.g., data exfiltration, remote access).

behavioral_signatures: Platform-specific wheels uploaded after initial release
Wheels with content differing from the source distribution
Install-time code execution or dependency changes only in certain wheels
file_indicators: Wheels uploaded significantly after the main release
Wheels with unique dependencies not present in the source
network_indicators: Outbound network connections during install-time from pip or setup.py
Unexpected domains contacted by installation scripts
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor all artifacts (wheels and source distributions) for each release. Compare the content and dependencies of each wheel to the source distribution. Flag any wheels uploaded after the initial release window, especially those that are highly platform-specific or contain unique code/dependencies. Use hash-checking mode in pip or lockfiles (Pipfile.lock) to ensure only known-good artifacts are installed. Monitor for install-time network activity or filesystem changes originating from package installation.
